explanations: terra: The losers “break God’s covenant” after its confirmation; this recurrent Qur’anic n-q-ḍ sense provides a lexical boundary for the rarer joint-sound sense developed in the section.
terra: The section’s dictionary definition glosses setting down with ḥaṭṭ; the commanded word حِطَّةٌ is followed by forgiveness, joining the physical language of lowering to remission of faults.
terra: God raises the Mount above Israel while commanding them to hold revelation firmly; a massive weight is suspended over the addressees rather than removed from them.
terra: The one whose sin encompasses him belongs to the Fire; guilt is pictured as surrounding the person rather than sitting on the back, another concrete relation between wrongdoing and body.
terra: The repeated raising of the Mount above Israel accompanies a covenant they answer with disobedience; it contrasts an overhead coercive mass with the section’s relieved body and raised honor.
terra: A group casts God’s Book “behind their backs”; instead of God taking a burden off the back and raising dhikr, people themselves put revelation behind the back and reject it.

luna: The section's dictionary note for rafaʿ includes physically lifting with a cord and hand; this ayah depicts Abraham and Ishmael raising the foundations of the House. It gives the root's concrete lifting action a building scene, while 94:4 applies it to remembrance.
terra: In the fasting ruling, God desires ease and not hardship; this gives a concrete legal setting for divine relief rather than leaving the section’s lightening as an abstract promise.
terra: Within nursing and family support, no soul is charged beyond capacity and neither parent is to be harmed through the child; it applies the load boundary to an embodied care burden.
terra: God raises some messengers in degrees above others; the same root moves from physical lifting to prophetic rank, the semantic move required when the section raises a name.

luna: The section's load is taken off its carrier; here believers pray, “رَبَّنَا وَلَا تَحْمِلْ عَلَيْنَا إِصْرًا,” asking that a heavy burden not be laid on them. It turns the removal image into a communal plea against imposed weight. | terra: The prayer asks, “Do not load upon us a burden” (لَا تَحْمِلْ عَلَيْنَا إِصْرًا), while the ayah first says no soul is charged beyond capacity; it turns the section’s relieved weight into a communal plea to the same Lord.
terra: Mary’s mother says that when she “put her down” she was female; childbirth supplies another bodily use of the section’s وضع root, though this ayah does not itself call the pregnancy a load.
terra: God tells Jesus, “I am raising you to Me”; the same divine act toward a prophet raises the person rather than the person’s remembrance, marking a concrete lexical boundary.

terra: What misers withhold will be made a collar around their necks on Resurrection Day; possessions turn into bodily restraint, bringing moral liability close to the section’s load-and-fetter meeting.
terra: Those charged to explain scripture cast it behind their backs for a small price; the back becomes the place where remembrance is discarded, clarifying the moral opposite of raised remembrance.

luna: The section's wording “from you” presents weight taken off its bearer; this ayah says God wants to lighten things for people because the human being was created weak. It states the same concern for human capacity without naming the particular burden. | terra: “God desires to lighten from you” because the human was created weak; this states directly what the section makes audible through a back strained until its load is removed.
terra: The Prophet is told to fight while being charged only for himself and to urge the believers; his mission includes leadership, but his accountable burden cannot be reassigned to the group.

terra: The sick or rain-struck fighters may “put down your weapons” (تَضَعُوا أَسْلِحَتَكُمْ); the named verb denotes literal relief from carried equipment while the command preserves necessary caution.
terra: Whoever earns a fault and throws it onto an innocent person has “borne slander and manifest sin”; attempted transfer increases the accuser’s own burden rather than moving guilt away.
terra: The Mount is raised above the People of the Book for their covenant, making elevation threatening when the lifted object is a mountain over human bodies rather than a name for someone.
terra: Israel’s breaking of its covenant again uses n-q-ḍ for violation, not the audible result of weight; the distinction prevents the back in the section from being said to have been broken.

terra: “God raised him to Himself” again applies رفع to Jesus’s person; it clarifies that prophetic elevation can mean removal of the person, whereas the section explicitly names dhikr as the lifted object.
terra: After purification rules, God says He does not desire to place hardship upon believers; the statement sets a boundary between divine command and a crushing burden.
terra: Because they broke their covenant, hearts are hardened; the moral rupture belongs to this ayah’s context and contrasts with the section’s bodily creak under load.

terra: Abel tells his brother that the attacker will return bearing the liability of both the intended murder and his own sin; this is accrued responsibility, not an innocent person volunteering to absorb another’s guilt.

terra: The accusation that God’s hand is fettered is answered by saying the accusers’ hands are fettered while His hands are outspread; the polemic uses bodily restraint to distinguish constricted giving from divine generosity.

luna: The section's named lexeme vizr links sin with physical weight and names zahr as the back; when the Hour catches the deniers, “يَحْمِلُونَ أَوْزَارَهُمْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ.” Their sins remain on their backs, reversing the removed load. | terra: Those surprised by the Hour carry “their burdens upon their backs” (أَوْزَارَهُمْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ); vizr and zahr form the section’s exact bodily scene, but the load remains instead of being taken off.
terra: After recounting Abraham’s argument, God says, “We raise in degrees whom We will”; the named root denotes conferred rank, helping distinguish the raised remembrance from physical lifting.

luna: The section's first bodily image is an opened chest; here God expands the chest of the one He guides toward Islam and makes the disbeliever's chest tight. The same bodily site carries receptivity or constriction, clarifying the spiritual context of opening. | terra: God expands the breast of the one guided, but makes the breast of one led astray tight and constricted as though climbing into the sky; the same bodily site displays both relief and crushing resistance.
terra: The ayah refers to fat “carried by their backs”; it shares back-and-carrying anatomy but describes tissue on animals, so it serves only as a lexical boundary around the section’s burden scene.
terra: The commands concerning an orphan’s property and just measure are followed by “We charge no soul except to its capacity”; moral duty is measured rather than made crushing.

luna: The section's named lexeme vizr is also used in this rule the Prophet is told to state: no bearer carries another's burden. In its own context it grounds each soul's accountability, bounding the section's removal as God's act rather than a person's substitution. | terra: The Prophet is told to ask whether he should seek a lord other than God when every soul earns against itself and no bearer bears another’s vizr; this directly states the individual-accountability boundary behind the removed load.
terra: God raises some people above others in degrees in order to test them in what He gave; elevation is rank joined to responsibility, not release from accountability.
terra: Those whose scales are heavy are successful; moral heaviness in a just balance is favorable, reversing the section’s harmful heaviness on a back.
terra: Those whose scales are light lose themselves; this ayah completes 7:8’s reversal by showing that lightness can be ruinous when what is weighed is righteous worth rather than a carried burden.
terra: Those who believe and act rightly enter the Garden after the reminder that no soul is charged beyond capacity; attainable obligation stands against a back-breaking load.

luna: The section's named waḍaʿa root and wording “from them” describe taking a burden off its bearer; here the Prophet “يَضَعُ عَنْهُمْ” people's burdens and fetters. This extends the same relief to a community, though these restraints need not be the same guilt-load. | terra: The unlettered messenger “lays down from them their burden and the shackles” (يَضَعُ عَنْهُمْ إِصْرَهُمْ وَالْأَغْلَالَ), repeating the section’s verb, preposition, removal from a person, and secondary fetter image while making the relieved addressee a reliever of others.
terra: The repeated command to say حِطَّةٌ at the gate again makes “lowering/remission” the spoken route to sins being forgiven, matching the section’s movement from weight to guilt and release.
terra: The mountain is torn up above the people like a canopy and they think it will fall upon them; this is the section’s load relation reversed into an enormous weight poised overhead.
terra: God could have raised the man by His signs, but he clings to the earth and follows desire; upward exaltation is refused for downward attachment, clarifying the moral force of a raised name.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss for vizr begins with a physical load; in this ayah a spouse carries a light pregnancy that later becomes heavy. The load is internal rather than on the back, so this is a limited parallel in how bodily weight grows. | terra: A pregnancy begins as a light load and then grows heavy; the progression lets weight be known through the bearer’s changing bodily condition, as the section knows the unnamed load through the back’s strain.
terra: People who repeatedly break their treaty use n-q-ḍ for recurring betrayal; that agency and moral object differ from a load causing a passive back to sound.
terra: God promises to heal the breasts of believers through victory; the front of the body is made the felt site of relief, paralleling the section’s opened breast and relieved back.
terra: After 9:14’s healing of believers’ breasts, God removes the rage of their hearts; this ayah’s own contribution is the taking away of an inward weight.

luna: The section's dictionary picture begins with possessions carried as a load and turns vizr toward sin; here hoarded gold and silver are heated and used to brand foreheads, sides, and backs. It does not say they carry the wealth, so the specific link is wealth turning into a bodily mark, not a carried burden. | terra: Hoarded metal brands foreheads, sides, and backs; stored goods become bodily punishment on the back, a concrete moral transformation of possessions into weight and pain.
terra: Believers are told to go forth “light and heavy”; duty continues across bodily and material conditions, setting carried difficulty beside the section’s divinely relieved mission.
terra: Those who ask the Prophet for transport leave weeping when he has nothing on which to carry them; the ayah reverses the burden scene into people needing a bearer so they can join the task.

terra: The Messenger is described as deeply distressed by the believers’ suffering and solicitous for them; this specific concern may help explain prophetic weight, but it cannot specify the unnamed vizr.
terra: Revelation is called healing for what is in the breasts; it links dhikr-like instruction with inward relief at the same bodily site named at the section’s front.

terra: The Prophet is warned that his breast may be constricted by demands and rejection of revelation; the ayah supplies a specific pressure of mission without claiming that it exhausts the section’s deliberately unnamed vizr.
terra: Shuʿayb tells his people they have taken God “behind your backs” as something disregarded; it uses the rear of the body for neglect rather than for a load mercifully removed.

terra: Joseph orders his men to put the brothers’ merchandise inside their saddlebags; this plausibly recalls the section’s dictionary bundle filled with goods, though the ayah does not call the baggage a vizr or stress its weight.

terra: The brothers open their baggage and find their merchandise returned; it continues 12:62’s packed-goods scene and illustrates the portable object behind the dictionary sense, but not bodily strain.

terra: The drinking cup is placed in the brother’s saddlebag; object, container, and carriage closely match the mechanics of the section’s bundle definition, though the purpose is concealment rather than burden.

luna: The section's dictionary picture is a bundle of possessions carried as a load; in the cup-search, the reward offered is “حِمْلُ بَعِيرٍ,” a camel's load. This is a concrete cargo measure, though its context is a promised reward rather than a burden removed. | terra: A camel-load is offered for recovery of the missing cup; this names a measured cargo as reward, a plausible literal comparator for vizr before its moral extension.
terra: In Joseph’s story God says, “We raise in degrees whom We will”; the rise in standing follows divinely given wisdom and parallels remembrance elevated as honor.
terra: Joseph raises his parents upon the throne; the physical act also enacts public honor, bridging literal lifting and the section’s metaphorical elevation of a name.

luna: The section's dictionary detail pictures a prisoner's cord lifting a fetter; this ayah puts chains around the necks of people who deny resurrection. Its own contribution is restraint retained as judgment, opposite the section's removal of burden. | terra: The deniers have shackles around their necks; this literalizes the restraint adjacent to the section’s dictionary cord and contrasts with a burden already removed.
terra: Those of understanding do not break the covenant (لَا يَنقُضُونَ الْمِيثَاقَ); this negative covenant sense contrasts with the section’s specialized sound of a burdened back.
terra: Those who break God’s covenant use n-q-ḍ in the transgressive covenant sense; the shared root but different action helps preserve the creaking, not covenant-breaking, of the section’s back.
terra: Criminals are seen bound together in fetters; the image supplies an eschatological instance of the pranga-like restraint developed secondarily in the section.

luna: The Prophet's chest is described as tight because of what people say; this reverses the section's opened chest. The next ayah, 15:98, directs him to glorify his Lord and prostrate, completing the passage's response to that distress. | terra: God knows the Prophet’s breast is constricted by what opponents say; this remembered pressure gives a concrete contrary state to the expanded front and relieved back.

luna: The section develops the literal sense of a load borne on a back; this ayah says livestock carry people's loads to distant lands they could not reach without hardship. It places bodily weight within travel and the mercy of being carried. | terra: Livestock carry people’s heavy loads to a land they could reach only with great bodily strain; the scene makes the hardship of bearing weight visible without moralizing the cargo.

luna: The section's vizr is a sin-load taken off its bearer; here those who mislead will bear their own full burdens and additional burdens from those they misled. The image reverses relief into an added consequence for leading others astray. | terra: Misleaders carry their own awzār in full and some of the burdens of those they mislead; the ayah distinguishes personal guilt from the added liability caused by making others stray.
terra: “Do not break the oaths” uses n-q-ḍ for violating a binding commitment; the contrast guards the section’s أَنقَضَ from being flattened into moral breach instead of audible bodily strain.

terra: The woman who undoes her spun yarn after strength uses the named n-q-ḍ root for physical unravelling; this differs from the section’s branch in which the same root makes a weighted joint audibly creak rather than saying it broke.

luna: The section's image opens the Prophet's chest as relief; this ayah describes someone who opens his breast to disbelief, a contrary use of the same bodily image. It marks that an opened chest's meaning depends on what it receives. | terra: A person who “opens his breast to disbelief” uses bodily expansion for willing unbelief, setting a moral boundary around the section’s gracious expansion and preventing openness itself from being treated as automatically good.
terra: Each person’s fate is fastened to his neck and a record is brought out for him; personal accountability is attached to the body as concretely as the section’s burden rests on the back.

luna: The section's vizr is a burden removed from its bearer; this ayah says no bearer bears another's burden, then ties guidance to each soul and says punishment waits for a messenger. The personal-responsibility rule marks the opposite boundary. | terra: Guidance and straying accrue to the person, and “no bearer bears another’s burden”; this occurrence grounds the burden rule in each person’s response to guidance.

terra: The hand must be neither shackled to the neck nor spread to its furthest reach; this bodily restraint gives the section’s fetter image an ethical boundary between paralysis and ruinous release.
terra: The Prophet is promised that his Lord may raise him to a praised station; bestowed elevation and public praise directly parallel a remembrance raised for him.

terra: The Prophet may nearly consume himself in grief because people do not believe; this supplies a specific bodily strain that could belong among the unnamed pressures behind the image, though the section does not equate it with the vizr.
terra: The record is “set down” and criminals fear what it contains; the named placing verb moves from unloading a body to presenting the complete account of the deeds that make a moral burden.
terra: God grants Abraham and his family “a lofty tongue of truth,” an enduring honorable reputation that directly parallels a remembrance raised for the prophetic addressee.

luna: The section says the Prophet's remembrance is raised; this ayah says God raised Idris to a high station. Its own image is the elevation of a prophet's standing, not his name. | terra: God raises Idris to a high station; personal exaltation rather than cargo-lifting helps define the honor sense of the section’s fourth-ayah verb.

terra: The heavens almost rupture, the earth splits, and mountains collapse; this may parallel the section’s weight becoming perceptible through a bearer’s physical failure, though 19:91 supplies a blasphemous claim rather than an actual carried object.
terra: The cause of 19:90’s cosmic strain is the claim that the Merciful has taken a son; its own contribution is the intolerable utterance, making the parallel to a back-straining load indirect.
terra: God made the revelation easy in the Prophet’s tongue for glad tidings and warning; it specifies communicative ease in the mission whose strain the section recalls.

luna: The section portrays a load removed from the Prophet; this ayah sets a boundary on the mission's hardship, saying the Quran was not sent to make him suffer. Its own contribution is the stated purpose of the revelation, not another named load. | terra: “We did not send down the Qur’an upon you that you should suffer”; descent “upon” the Prophet does not make revelation the harmful weight the section says was taken “from” him.

luna: The section opens with the body's front, the chest, alongside the burdened back; Moses asks, “رَبِّ اشْرَحْ لِي صَدْرِي.” The next ayah, 20:26, completes his request by asking ease for his task, joining chest-opening to capacity for a mission. | terra: Moses asks, “My Lord, expand for me my breast” (اشْرَحْ لِي صَدْرِي); it is the clearest other prophetic plea for the bodily opening recalled at the front of this section.

luna: This continuation asks God to make Moses' task easy, following his request for an expanded chest in 20:25. Its own contribution links relief in the work to the preceding bodily image of an opened chest. | terra: Moses next asks God to ease his task; the ayah states as a request what the section’s taken-off load makes perceptible in the Prophet’s mission.
terra: Moses asks God to appoint a wazīr from his family; the shared w-z-r root has become a helper in responsibility, establishing a boundary between help with a mission and transfer of moral guilt.
terra: Moses asks that his strength be reinforced through Aaron; this bodily language explains what the requested wazīr of 20:29 contributes without claiming that Aaron bears Moses’s personal vizr.
terra: Moses asks that Aaron share in his task; shared work provides the positive counterpart to the impossible proposal that someone assume another person’s guilt.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss for vizr includes goods packed and carried; after the calf episode, the people say they were loaded with “أَوْزَارًا مِّن زِينَةِ الْقَوْمِ.” Here awzār means actual ornaments, preserving the concrete sense before the section's move to sin as a load. | terra: The calf-makers say they were made to carry awzār from the people’s ornaments; these are portable goods, giving the Qur’anic concrete baseline for the section’s cloth bundle before vizr becomes moral weight.

luna: The section's named vizr as a sin-load is left behind by its addressee; here the one who turns away from the Reminder “يَحْمِلُ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ وِزْرًا.” This is the inverse: turning from remembrance leaves a burden to carry. | terra: The one who turns away from the Reminder carries a vizr on Resurrection Day; it directly reverses the section’s movement in which the vizr is removed and dhikr is raised.

luna: Following 20:100's burden for turning away from the Reminder, this ayah calls the coming weight “حِمْلًا” and says it is a bad load for them. Its own contribution is to make the burden's outcome explicit, opposite the load's removal. | terra: Following 20:100’s bearer, this ayah calls the carried thing an evil load (حِمْلًا), supplying the felt weight of the vizr that refusal of remembrance leaves in place.

terra: God says He sent down a Book “in which is your dhikr”; whether read as reminder or honor, it locates the audience’s standing in revelation and provides a communal analogue to the Prophet’s raised dhikr.
terra: God “sets down the just balances” for Resurrection, so no soul is wronged; placing here begins exact moral weighing rather than relieving a bearer.

luna: The section's named waḍaʿa root means lowering or putting down a load; at the terror of the Hour this ayah says every pregnant woman will put down what she carries. It is a literal bodily load released by terror, opposite the section's relief. | terra: At the Hour every pregnant one “puts down her load” (تَضَعُ كُلُّ ذَاتِ حَمْلٍ حَمْلَهَا); the same bodily verb-object relation makes the release sudden and overwhelming.
terra: Believers are told to strive while being reminded that God placed no constriction upon them in religion; duty remains, but it is not the back-breaking weight of the section.
terra: People are carried on livestock and ships; the human body becomes cargo rather than bearer, a useful reversal of the section’s person under a load.
terra: God charges no soul beyond capacity, and a record with Him speaks truth; measured burden and exact accounting meet in the same ayah.
terra: Those whose scales are heavy prosper; the repeated judgment formula keeps beneficial moral weight distinct from an oppressive load.
terra: Those whose scales are light lose themselves in Hell; the result confirms that relief from a bodily burden and deficiency in the balance are opposite kinds of lightness.

luna: The section's raised remembrance is paired here with houses God permits “أَن تُرْفَعَ” and where “اسْمُهُ” is remembered. The raised place and remembered name meet in one scene, though the ayah concerns houses of worship rather than the Prophet's mention. | terra: God permits houses “to be raised” and His name to be remembered in them; elevation and dhikr meet in one ayah, closely paralleling the raising of the addressee’s remembrance.

terra: Elderly women may lay aside their outer garments without displaying adornment; garment and the named setting-down verb meet here, but unlike the section’s dictionary bundle the garment is neither filled nor carried.

luna: The section's dictionary detail involves a prisoner and his fetter; this ayah depicts criminals thrown into a narrow place while bound together. The restraint remains in place, the contrary state to the section's load being taken off. | terra: The condemned are thrown into a narrow place bound together; confinement and binding show the bodily opposite of the section’s opening and unloading.
terra: God gives Moses the Book and makes his brother Aaron a wazīr with him; revelation’s heavy task has a companion-helper even though accountable burdens remain personal.
terra: The Prophet may nearly destroy himself because the people are not believers; the intense mission-grief is a plausible component of back-breaking pressure, but no load vocabulary is used.

luna: The section presents an opened chest at the front of the body; Moses says his chest tightens and his tongue is not fluent as he faces Pharaoh. This is a specific reversal of the opened-chest image under the strain of a prophetic task. | terra: Moses says his breast constricts and his tongue does not move freely, then asks that Aaron be sent; mission-pressure, bodily constriction, speech, and assistance meet in one prophetic complaint.
terra: Abraham asks for “a tongue of truth among later people”; the prayer names the lasting good mention that the section describes spatially as raised dhikr.
terra: Moses asks that his more eloquent brother be sent as support who confirms him; the verse specifies speech and assistance as shareable burdens of mission.
terra: God promises to strengthen Moses’s arm through his brother; bodily support supplies a concrete alternative to a back left creaking alone under a task.

luna: This ayah's contribution is the unbelievers' false offer to carry the believers' errors if they follow their way; 29:13 answers it. The section's named burden-transfer image thus meets an explicit, rejected promise to take another's load. | terra: The unbelievers say, “Follow our way, and we will carry your errors”; this voiced offer stages precisely the impossible substitute bearer that 29:13 and the section’s cited rule correct.

luna: This ayah answers the offer in 29:12: the deceivers will indeed bear their own burdens and further burdens alongside them. It clarifies that misleaders add liability through their own act; they do not simply substitute for those they misled. | terra: After the empty offer in 29:12, the misleaders really do carry their own weights and further weights with them; the addition is causal liability, not the innocent transfer forbidden by the section’s burden rule.
terra: A mother carries her child “in weakness upon weakness”; the cumulative bodily strain corresponds to the section’s weight known through what it does to the bearer.
terra: God and His angels bless the Prophet and believers are commanded to bless and greet him; the ayah enacts his elevated remembrance across divine, angelic, and human speech.
terra: Those who harm innocent believers “bear slander and manifest sin”; the verb turns wrongful injury into a moral weight retained by the perpetrator.

luna: The section does not identify the burden on the Prophet's back; this ayah names a distinct trust that the heavens, earth, and mountains declined and the human being carried, “وَحَمَلَهَا الْإِنسَانُ.” It gives a separate image of weighty responsibility rather than identifying the removed load. | terra: The heavens, earth, and mountains refuse the Trust, while the human carries it; this is the Qur’an’s largest contrast between an entrusted weight that must be borne and the unnamed weight that is removed.

luna: The section connects misleaders with extra burdens carried at judgment; in this ayah the misled and their arrogant leaders dispute blame, then shackles are placed on the disbelievers' necks. It joins misguidance with a distinct restraint scene rather than transferring the load. | terra: Shackles are put around the necks of the disbelievers as recompense for what they did; moral consequence becomes a physical restraint borne by the body.
terra: The Prophet is told not to let his soul depart in regrets over the misled; it names a burdening grief that divine address restrains, while leaving the link to the section’s load conjectural.

luna: The section's named rafaʿ wording raises remembrance; here good speech ascends to God and righteous deeds are said to raise it, “وَالْعَمَلُ الصَّالِحُ يَرْفَعُهُ.” This gives spoken good and its elevation a parallel, with God as the destination. | terra: Good speech ascends to God and righteous action raises it; verbal remembrance acquires upward movement, clarifying that the section’s raised “name” is honor and accepted speech rather than a lifted object.

terra: No female conceives or gives birth except with God’s knowledge; “puts down” retains the bodily delivery sense, but without an explicit load or hardship the correspondence is thinner than 46:15 and 65:4.

luna: The section's named vizr connects sin to weight; this judgment rule says “وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ,” and even a heavily loaded soul gets no part of its burden carried. It sets the limit that one person's guilt is not removed by another human, unlike God's removal in the section. | terra: “No bearer bears another’s burden,” and even a heavily laden soul that calls for help has none of it carried; this gives the rule against transferred liability that makes the section’s divine removal exceptional without making God another accountable bearer.

luna: The section's dictionary note describes a bound person lifting a fetter's cord; this ayah places collars on necks up to the chins, leaving the people with their heads held up. Its own image is a posture forced by fetters, opposite a restraint being lifted by its bearer. | terra: Shackles rise to the unbelievers’ chins so their heads are forced up; this literal restraint closely realizes the section’s dictionary image of a bound person holding up the cord of his fetter, while distinguishing forced elevation from raised honor.
terra: God carries human progeny in a laden ship; both vessel and passengers participate in bearing, widening the section’s carrier-load relation beyond a human back.
terra: God leaves Noah a remembrance among later generations; this lasting presence after him is a concrete nonlexical parallel to having one’s dhikr raised.
terra: “Peace upon Noah among the worlds” supplies the honored words preserved by 37:78’s remembrance, showing what an elevated name sounds like in later mouths.
terra: God leaves Abraham a remembrance among later generations, fulfilling the prayer for lasting truthful mention and paralleling the section’s raised dhikr.
terra: “Peace upon Abraham” gives the content of 37:108’s surviving remembrance and thus an enacted example of an honored prophetic name.
terra: God leaves Moses and Aaron a remembrance among later generations; the plural pair shows that enduring honor can attach to co-workers in a burdened mission.
terra: “Peace upon Moses and Aaron” voices the memorial preserved in 37:119, making raised remembrance audible rather than spatial.
terra: God leaves Elijah a remembrance among later generations, repeating the pattern in which divine speech sustains a prophet’s honorable name.
terra: “Peace upon Ilyāsīn” states the remembered greeting promised by 37:129 and gives another concrete form of elevated mention.
terra: Others are bound together in fetters under Solomon’s control; unlike punitive burdens borne at judgment, these bonds belong to a scene of constrained labor and rule.

luna: This ayah repeats the section's named vizr formula that no bearer carries another's burden, while saying God has no need of disbelief and is pleased with gratitude. Its context underscores personal answerability rather than a transferable load. | terra: Within the contrast between disbelief and gratitude, the ayah says no bearer bears another’s vizr; it ties the image’s weight to one’s own stance toward God rather than transferable cargo.

luna: This ayah describes a person whose chest God has expanded for Islam and who is then upon light from his Lord. It parallels the section's opened chest as a change in inward capacity, while naming guidance as its context. | terra: The one whose breast God expands for submission stands in divine light, while the ayah ends with hard hearts; it gives the opened front of the body a spiritual consequence that complements the relieved back.

terra: The best speech makes the skins of those who fear God shiver, then their skins and hearts soften to God’s remembrance; like the creaking back, meaning becomes perceptible through bodily response, but here dhikr ends in softness.
terra: At judgment the Book is set down and prophets and witnesses are brought; the same verb introduces disclosure and just decision, showing that not every وضع is release.
terra: The Prophet is commanded to seek forgiveness for his dhanb; this is relevant only to the section’s secondary “vizr as sin” sense and should not be used to name the unspecified burden.

luna: The section's dictionary detail links a prisoner's raised fetter-cord to restraint; this ayah pictures collars on necks and chains as people are dragged. Its own contribution is a body still bound at judgment, reversing the release image. | terra: With collars around their necks and chains, the deniers are dragged; the ayah closely supplies the hard restraint evoked by the section’s fetter cord.
terra: Following 40:71’s collars and chains, this ayah makes the bound bodies be dragged into boiling water and fire; its own contribution is the forced movement imposed by the restraint.

terra: People reach needs held in their breasts by means of livestock, and are carried on them and on ships; chest, need, and being borne meet in one ayah, reversing the section’s human bearer into a carried passenger.
terra: No female bears or gives birth without God’s knowledge; the carrying-and-delivery pair faintly parallels a burden put down, though its point is divine knowledge rather than relief.

terra: The heavens nearly split from above while angels glorify God; cosmic strain and raised praise meet suggestively with the section’s creaking weight and dhikr, but the ayah does not identify a burden.

luna: The section's image places weight on a person's back; this ayah says people sit on the backs of cattle and ships, then recalls God's favor in carrying them. Its own contribution reverses the bearer: an animal's back supports the person rather than the person's back bearing a load. | terra: Humans settle on the backs of mounts and glorify the One who subjected them; the ayah reverses the carrier perspective—humans become the load—and joins a back with spoken remembrance.

luna: The section's raised object is the Prophet's remembrance; this ayah speaks of God raising some people above others in degrees as livelihood is apportioned. It contrasts elevated mention with worldly rank and provision. | terra: God raises some people above others in degrees so they may employ one another; this social differentiation is another real sense of رفع and sets a boundary around the section’s personal honor.
terra: The Qur’an is “a dhikr for you and your people,” addressing the Prophet with the same word that the section says God raised for him and locating that honor in revelation.
terra: God says He made the Qur’an easy in the Prophet’s tongue so that people might remember; ease, the same addressee, speech, and remembrance meet explicitly.

luna: The section's image makes weight borne by a body audible on the back; this ayah says a mother carried her child with hardship and delivered him with hardship. Its own contribution is a distinct bodily burden at pregnancy and birth, not a guilt-load or a back-load. | terra: A mother carries her child in hardship and puts it down in hardship (حَمَلَتْهُ ... وَوَضَعَتْهُ), a bodily instance in which carrying ends through the section’s named act of setting down.

terra: The section sets a vizr down; here war itself “lays down its burdens” (تَضَعَ الْحَرْبُ أَوْزَارَهَا), joining both named roots in one concrete idiom and showing that awzār can be the weight and equipment of conflict rather than personal sin.
terra: The command to seek forgiveness for the Prophet’s dhanb and for believers may illuminate one possible moral sense of a removed vizr, but the lexical and contextual bridge remains indirect.

terra: God’s promised forgiveness of the Prophet’s earlier and later dhanb may meet the dictionary path from vizr to sin and divine removal, but the section itself refuses to identify its load as a particular fault.
terra: God promises the Prophet mighty help; this supplies direct divine support for the mission alongside 48:2’s forgiveness and the section’s removed strain.
terra: Believers must not raise their voices above the Prophet’s voice; human vocal elevation over him is forbidden even as God raises his remembrance, distinguishing honor from loudness.
terra: The oath by “those bearing a load” evokes carriers under weight, perhaps winds or clouds; the relation is concrete, but the bearers are not identified in the ayah and no relief occurs.

terra: God joins believing descendants to their families without diminishing anyone’s deeds, then says each person is held in pledge for what he earned; gracious reunion does not transfer accountable burdens.

luna: The section's named vizr formula appears in the account of what was made known to Moses and Abraham: no bearer bears another's burden. This places the removal image beside a repeated rule of individual liability. | terra: The scrolls of Moses and Abraham contain the rule that no bearer bears another’s vizr, locating the section’s burden boundary in an older revealed teaching.

luna: Immediately after 53:38 says one bearer does not carry another's burden, this ayah says a person has only what they strive for. Its own contribution is to connect the load rule with responsibility for one's effort. | terra: Immediately after 53:38’s rule that no bearer bears another’s burden, this ayah adds that a human has only what he strives for; it specifies the positive ownership corresponding to nontransferable liability.
terra: “We have made the Qur’an easy for remembrance”; the same divine plural joins ease to dhikr, showing how the “heavy word” can be accessible once given.
terra: The repeated declaration that God made the Qur’an easy for remembrance reinforces that revelatory weight does not entail disabling hardship.
terra: This third occurrence again couples divine facilitation with dhikr, a direct thematic meeting of the load removed and remembrance raised.
terra: The fourth repeated assurance preserves the same ease-and-remembrance relation after successive warning narratives.

terra: God “raised” the sky and “set” the balance (رَفَعَهَا وَوَضَعَ الْمِيزَانَ); the two named roots appear together, making the section’s load-down/name-up movement part of an ordered vertical pair.
terra: After 55:7 raises the sky and sets the balance, God “lays out” the earth for creatures; it extends the vertical ordering of the same وضع root from instrument to habitable ground.
terra: The Event is “abasing, raising” (خَافِضَةٌ رَّافِعَةٌ); its paired reversals show that elevation may be judgment and rank, not merely the mechanical opposite of setting down a load.

terra: The ẓihār formula derives its force from calling a wife like one’s mother’s back, yet the ayah rejects that speech as false; the same back root has a legal-idiomatic use wholly different from a load-bearing back.

terra: One who returns after ẓihār must free an enslaved person before marital contact; the back-derived formula of 58:2 is answered with release from bodily bondage, joining two of the section’s secondary details.

luna: The section's named rafaʿ image makes remembrance rise; this ayah says God raises believers and those given knowledge in degrees. It offers a specific parallel of elevated standing while naming faith and knowledge as its measure. | terra: God raises believers and people of knowledge in degrees; this shared root explicitly means granted rank, supporting the reading of raised remembrance as bestowed honor.

terra: Had the Qur’an descended on a mountain, it would have humbled and split from fear of God; alongside 73:5’s heavy word, this offers a possible image for revelation’s felt weight, while the section deliberately leaves its vizr unnamed.

luna: The section's load is bodily weight; this ayah compares those entrusted with Torah who do not carry it out to a donkey carrying books, “يَحْمِلُ أَسْفَارًا.” The physical load remains while its intended responsibility is unmet. | terra: The donkey carrying books stages a back loaded with revelation that the bearer does not comprehend; it sharply separates physically bearing scripture from the raised, living dhikr in the section.
terra: For pregnant women the term lasts until “they put down their load” (يَضَعْنَ حَمْلَهُنَّ), an ordinary embodied counterpart to a weight being taken from its bearer.
terra: The command to maintain pregnant women until they put down their load repeats the concrete carrying-and-release scene while attaching duties of care to it.
terra: God charges a soul only according to what He has given it and “will make after hardship ease”; capacity, load, and the surah’s ensuing promise of ease converge in one rule.
terra: God directly clears the Prophet of the accusation of madness by His grace; the defense restores the addressee’s public name, a specific aspect of elevated remembrance.
terra: The promise of an unfailing reward follows the defense in 68:2; its own contribution is enduring divine recompense accompanying restored honor.
terra: God declares the Prophet to possess tremendous character; this positive divine testimony supplies the honored reputation raised above the slander rejected in 68:2.

luna: The section's dictionary note evokes the prisoner's hand lifting the cord of a fetter; this ayah commands that a condemned man be seized and shackled. Its own contribution is the act of binding, the contrary state to a load or restraint taken off. | terra: The command “seize him and shackle him” makes fastening the guilty body an explicit spoken judgment, the inverse action to taking a burden off someone.

luna: The section's dictionary detail evokes a cord attached to a fetter; this ayah specifies a chain seventy cubits long into which the condemned man is thrust. The preceding punishment passage orders him shackled at 69:30; this ayah contributes the chain's length and continued restraint. | terra: A seventy-cubit chain is threaded through the condemned person; after the seizure in 69:30, this ayah specifies the extraordinary binding instrument itself.

luna: The section leaves the removed burden unnamed; the same divine “We” tells the Prophet, “قَوْلًا ثَقِيلًا” will be cast upon him. A heavy revelation commission can coexist with relief from another burden. | terra: The same divine “We” promises to cast upon the Prophet “a heavy word” (قَوْلًا ثَقِيلًا); it marks the boundary between a disabling burden removed from him and the weighty revelation he is still entrusted to receive.

luna: The section develops a prisoner's fetter and the rope by which it is raised; this ayah names shackles and fire among the punishments prepared for its deniers. It supplies the retained-restraint side of the contrast. | terra: God warns of shackles and a blazing fire; the fetters show another possible weight laid upon bodies, set against the same surah’s “heavy word” entrusted to the Prophet.

terra: In the same surah that promises a heavy word, God knows the community cannot sustain the full night measure, turns toward them, and repeatedly commands recitation of what is easy; weight is retained while practice is lightened.
terra: “Every soul is held in pledge for what it earned”; personal deeds become bodily-seeming restraint, joining the section’s nontransferable moral load to its fetter image.

terra: The cry “no refuge” uses وَزَر in the sense of shelter, not the section’s وِزْر as load; the vocalized lexical boundary matters because the same consonants otherwise invite a false burden reading.

luna: The section's dictionary note describes a bound person's fetter; this ayah says chains and shackles have been prepared for the disbelievers. Its own contribution is explicit punishment by restraints, the inverse of restraints being removed. | terra: Chains, collars, and a blaze are prepared for rejecters; the clustered restraint vocabulary directly develops the section’s secondary pranga image.
terra: The honored pages of 80:13 are “raised and purified”; this ayah’s own contribution is elevation of the written Reminder itself, close to raised dhikr.
terra: The person given his record from behind his back embodies guilt at the rear of the body and proceeds toward ruin, reversing the addressee whose back has already been relieved.

luna: The section's dictionary account locates the back's creaking in joints and ribs; this creation ayah names the backbone and ribs as paired bodily landmarks. It concerns fluid and human creation, not weight or sound, so the link is anatomical only.
terra: “We shall ease you toward ease” is a divine plural promise to the Prophet, stating directly the ease embodied by taking a back-straining burden from him.
terra: Paradise contains couches “raised high”; beside the cups set down in 88:14, the physical arrangement instantiates the section’s lexical up/down pair, though on separate objects.
terra: Cups are “set out” (مَوْضُوعَةٌ) beside the raised couches of 88:13; the juxtaposition concretizes وضع against رفع without implying that the cups are burdens.
terra: On that Day none binds as God binds; divine fastening supplies a general judgment counterpart to the section’s concrete shackle and cord image.
terra: “Freeing a neck” is the direct humane reversal of the section’s cord, shackle, and burden imagery: restraint is physically undone at the body that bears it.
terra: The giver who fears God and affirms the best is “eased toward ease”; it generalizes the Prophet’s experienced lightening into a moral path open to others.
terra: The miser who denies the best is “eased toward hardship”; the paradox reverses the section’s relief and shows that being facilitated can lead toward a difficult end rather than release.
terra: The rhetorical reminder that God found the Prophet an orphan and sheltered him parallels the section’s retrospective question about a past vulnerability already relieved.
terra: The reminder that God found the Prophet searching and guided him adds another concrete before-and-after act in the same direct divine address.
terra: God found the Prophet in need and enriched him; relief from lack completes the preceding surah’s series of remembered divine interventions, analogous in stance to taking off the unnamed load.
terra: The earth brings out “its burdens”; a vast bearer discharges what was hidden inside it, giving a cosmic counterpart to a load leaving the human body.
terra: After the earth discharges its burdens and people are shown their deeds, whoever does an atom’s weight of good sees it; this ayah identifies one moral content disclosed from the hidden weight.
terra: Whoever does an atom’s weight of evil sees it; paired with 99:7, this makes moral weight exact and personal after the earth’s burdens emerge.
terra: The one whose scales are heavy enters a pleasing life; here weight signals sufficient good, not the damaging pressure heard in the section’s back.
terra: The one whose scales are light has the abyss as refuge; it supplies the adverse boundary showing that “light” is not invariably the Qur’anic image of salvation.
terra: The Prophet’s hater is the one cut off; that loss of posterity and mention supplies the personal reverse of the enduring remembrance raised for the addressee.
terra: The “carrier of firewood” turns carrying into a person’s defining posture and punishment, an adverse bodily counterpart to the addressee whose load has been removed.
terra: The rope of palm fibre around the carrier’s neck completes 111:4’s load scene and closely meets the section’s secondary image of a cord joined to restraint.
